questions.question: Define a species and use the example of the horse and the donkey to explain the definition.
questions.expected_answer: A species is a group of organisms of the same type that can breed together to produce fertile offspring. A horse and a donkey can mate, but their offspring, the mule, is almost always infertile, so horses and donkeys are separate species.

questions.question: Define variation and distinguish between continuous and discontinuous variation, giving two examples of each and the type of graph used.
questions.expected_answer: Variation is the differences between individuals of the same species. Continuous variation: the feature can take any value in a range, with gradual differences; examples height, mass, hand span, foot length; shown by a bar graph or histogram of grouped ranges that forms a bell shape. Discontinuous variation: the feature falls into distinct groups with no in-between values; examples blood group (A, B, AB, O), tongue rolling, attached or free earlobes; shown as a bar graph with separate bars.

questions.question: Explain the two causes of variation with an example of each, and explain why variation is important for a species.
questions.expected_answer: Inherited variation: caused by differences in genes received from parents; each parent passes on a random half, so offspring have new combinations (blood group, natural eye colour). Environmental variation: caused by conditions during life such as diet, climate, exercise or disease (scars, sun tan, size of a plant in poor soil); acquired features are not inherited. Many features, like height, are affected by both. Variation is important because if conditions change or a disease appears, some individuals may have features that let them survive and reproduce, so the species does not die out; it also allows breeders to select useful features.
